#1114. Leading ice hockey nations, sponsors oppose Russia's return

Ice hockey's governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia presents "significant practical and sporting challenges." Several leading nations say they won't play against Russian teams.

The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated."

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."

Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.

On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."

In a statement to DW on Wednesday, a German government spokesperson reiterated Berlin's position on the matter from the weekend, saying it viewed Friday's CAS ruling "very critically."

The spokesperson also said  the government would "consult with the German Ice Hockey Federation in the near future regarding the potential consequences of this decision, including its impact on the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany."

Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.

Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.

Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.

Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."

USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

On Wednesday afternoon, yet another sponsor joined the list, with German workwear company Strauss saying it would "forgo all logo exposure associated with the (men's) tournament" and was considering withdrawing its sponsporship entirely.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

This article was originally published on November 4, 2026. It was updated on November 5, 2026 with the German government statement to DW.

#1108. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

It is always worth remembering that you only get a true reading of the Premier League table after ten games so this is a pivotal moment for both Newcastle and Everton as they play their ninth match of the campaign.

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but big questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach.  It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Given all the problems attached to their summer recruitment - or rather the lack of it - Everton will have defied the grim pre-season predictions heading into the second international break. Newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

“It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

#1101. Gold for the West Bank: Meet Palestinian karate champ Mariam Bsharat

The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

"After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."

Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the Palestine national team in Poland in October.

"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

"I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat said. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed."

Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.

"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," said Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).

"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat said. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.

Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."

As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat said.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."

That has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.

"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.

"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."

The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

#1097. Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amber Dance is a freelance science writer near Los Angeles, California.

A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library

First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut. That’s a collection that ranks as ‘excellent’ according to NirvanaBiome, the company in Germantown, Maryland, that analysed my stool sample. The firm based its rating on the overall diversity of my gut’s residents plus my levels of specific beneficial and undesirable species.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

But then came a second, less promising assessment: Viome in Bellevue, Washington, identified only 61 kinds of active microorganism in my gut and suggested that some of them were not performing optimally. Viome recommended dietary changes and offered customized supplements to improve my health.

I was intrigued by the results, but also flummoxed by the different messages. That’s not an uncommon response, says microbiologist Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation at the University of California, San Diego. When scientists tested a handful of microbiome testing kits alongside one another in formal studies, they found wide discrepancies in the results. These differences make it hard to understand or really trust the findings from any given provider, says Diane Hoffmann, director of the Law and Health Care programme at the University of Maryland in Baltimore, who co-authored one of those studies.

The companies stand by their products. “Of course there’s variability,” says Kelly Moffat, chief operations officer for Cmbio in Germantown, which does the laboratory work and genetic sequencing for NirvanaBiome. “There has to be because this is complex testing.”

Momo Vuyisich, chief science officer at Viome’s lab in Bothwell, Washington, also says he was unsurprised by the degree of variation found by formal studies. Labs use different methods to extract, sequence and analyse microbial genetic material. Viome, for example, sequences RNA rather than DNA, allowing it to uncover microbial gene activity, rather than only the presence of genes. Vuyisich argues that this is more relevant to human health. And he says that although every method will have biases, as long as a consumer sticks with the same provider, it should produce results that are comparable over time.

Interest in these kinds of test is booming. “There’s so much public enthusiasm and excitement about the microbiome,” says Knight. Some customers are simply curious about the microscopic beings that live inside them and potentially affect their health; others have health conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and hope that their gut microbes will reveal the underlying cause or a path to better health.

Although people can order the tests and follow their recommendations without the help of a medical professional, some people are bringing the findings to their physicians. “I groan when I see someone come in with a microbiome test,” says Fergus Shanahan, a gastroenterologist and immunologist at University College Cork in Ireland, who has spent much of his career studying the microbiome. For someone struggling with gut health, a consumer microbiome profile isn’t usually specific enough to help. And if there’s a concern about an infection, such as Clostridioides difficile, it’s more straightforward to test for known pathogens than to assess the entire microbial community.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

Microbiologists and gasteroenterologists who spoke to Nature generally agreed that microbiome testing has the potential to both reflect and promote health, but many said that the science isn’t yet mature enough to support microbiome testing for most consumers. In their view, the limited clinical usefulness of today’s consumer tests can make them poor value for money (costing around US$100–300). The specialists warn that acting on advice that doesn’t come from clinicians could lead customers to adopt unnecessarily restrictive diets or delay appropriate medical assessment. Critics say that consumer microbiome testing needs more regulatory scrutiny and oversight.

“This is an industry that’s running wild,” says genomicist Jacques Ravel, director of the Center for Advanced Microbiome Research and Innovation at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore and a co-author on one of the studies that tested several providers. With regards to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”.

Moffat says, “I think the jury’s out on exactly what it is that we can actionably do today based on this data.” But she says that microbiome profiles, combined with other testing such as gut metabolomics, could yield interesting and useful health information.

The gut microbiome has emerged as an incredible correlate of overall health. From immune-system function to metabolism, skin disorders and mental health, study after study has found links between a person’s well-being and the trillions of microbes that live in their digestive tract. The premise of a head count of these species and assessment of their actions, to monitor and improve gut health in a personalized way, certainly sounds appealing. Viome’s website, for example, promises: “No more trial and error … Follow a plan built precisely for you.”

Companies can identify species and, on the basis of those lists, infer what the microbes are probably doing, such as manufacturing metabolites or inciting inflammation. But running even the simplest microbiome testing is expensive, says Alessandra Cervino, research director at PiLeJe, a science-based food-supplement company in Paris. She says her microbiome testing company, Luxia Scientific, closed in 2024 for financial reasons.

Some microbiome testing firms recommend fermented foods, such as kombucha, for gut health.Credit: Deb Lindsey for The Washington Post via Getty

Many testing companies also offer lifestyle and nutritional advice or sell supplements. For example, Viome analysed diverse functions performed by the microbes in my gut, such as digestive efficiency, gas production and serotonin manufacture. I then received a detailed eating plan — which told me to eschew broccoli and load up on pecans, among other suggestions — along with an offer for precision supplements and probiotics with a price tag of more than $150 a month. Although it’s hard to change the composition of microbes in one’s gut, alterations in diet or even simply ageing can shift their activities, says Vuyisich. The company recommends re-testing every four to six months to check for shifts and update the plan.

He points to 19 peer-reviewed publications by Viome as evidence of the company’s rigour (see go.nature.com/4actdhq). For example, the firm’s analysis for consumers is supported, in part, by published data on how gut microbes influence individuals’ responses to glucose in various foods, based on 550 people in the United States who collectively ate more than 30,000 meals while wearing glucose monitors1. The company validated those findings in a further cohort in Japan, Vuyisich says, but those data are not published.

Microbiome tests are not created equal, says Tim Spector, a physician-scientist at King’s College London and co-founder of London-based ZOE, which offers microbiome testing and a supplement in addition to a gut-health app that I’ve been playing with. ZOE’s products, Spector says, are backed by research on thousands of people. “There definitely are some not-so-good players out there that give this field a bad name,” he says. “It’s not easy to do this well.”

There are also several ways to do microbe testing; companies take varying approaches that yield disparate results, as at least two studies have shown. Scientists at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, Maryland, shipped homogenized stool samples from one person to seven companies2. NIST’s remit is researching and applying standards for measurement. This experiment was a step towards understanding the diversity of testing options out there, says one of the study authors, NIST microbiologist Stephanie Servetas, who is based in Sheridan, Wyoming. The researchers didn’t name the companies in their report because they wanted to focus attention on the comparison between tests rather than perceived accuracy of any individual provider.

The result: “Companies produce strikingly different results,” says co-author Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist who used to direct the NIST microbiology program and is now a consultant in Saint Michaels, Maryland. “They couldn’t even agree on what’s healthy and unhealthy,” Jackson says. The microbe lists ranged from 34 to 906 identified genera; only 3 of which showed up in all reports. In fact, the results were as varied from company to company as they would be for different people, despite all tests being done on samples from the same individual.

A European and Canadian team obtained similar outcomes when they sent homogenized samples from one person’s stool to six companies, also anonymized. Three companies rated the microbial diversity as “excellent” or “good”; two called it “average”; one said it was “unfavourable”3. The results were so variable, that at least some of them must be lacking in validation or standardization, says co-author Céline Druart, executive director of the Pharmabiotic Research Institute (PRI) in Brussels, a non-profit organization specializing in regulation of microbiome innovations. “It’s very difficult to make a conclusion,” she says.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

This broad divergence in results is not surprising, says Jack Gilbert, director of the Microbiome and Metagenomics Center at the University of California, San Diego. The variation starts at sampling: scoop a bit of faecal matter into a tube, stab it with a coring device or swipe the sampler across some used toilet paper; ship it off as-is, or in some kind of preservative (as both Viome’s and NirvanaBiome’s kits asked me to). Each option could influence the balance of the microbes that are collected and what survives to be sequenced.

In the lab, Servetas says the method by which the researchers extract genetic material from a sample is a big source of divergence. Gentler protocols will bias a sample towards microbes that are easy to crack open, whereas harsher methods will capture a higher share of species with tougher exteriors.

After sequencing, another major source of difference, says Knight, is the bioinformatics pipeline that labs use. What length or number of genetic sequences is required to consider a microbe present? What list of sequences and microbes are they using as a reference? “All bets are off when you then computationally analyse it with your favourite method,” says Knight.

Would companies support having standards to validate their tests? “We are really big advocates on really having a standard here,” says Kimberley Sukhum, chief science officer at Tiny Health in Austin, Texas, which offers gut microbiome tests as well as vaginal microbiome tests.

But it’s hard to set those standards, in part because there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample. Compare that with, say, a blood-glucose test; a lab can get a known value from a standard sample either right or wrong. But the microbiome, in its glorious complexity, does not allow for such simple validation. NIST has used mixed human donor samples to develop a standard4. And Tiny Health has experimented with generating a reference for benchmarking from synthetic communities. It was built from individual microbial species rather than sampled from faeces5. But neither of those standards is exactly like the microbiome of an individual person.

Even if labs could assess a microbiome perfectly, they’d still have a problem: there’s no defined healthy microbiome like there is one range of healthy blood-glucose levels. Each person’s microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. There are infinitely many ways to have a healthy microbiome, and infinitely many ways to have an unhealthy one, says Shanahan; it’s not entirely clear how to draw a line between the two.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

Companies must compare customer microbiomes with some standard of health, but these vary too. They might be based on past customers or large, public databases. But microbiomes differ considerably depending on factors such as ethnicity, sex, age, recent antibiotic use or even whether someone was born by caesarean section.

#1094. What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition.  Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

#1087. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he said.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

“It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was important to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

“It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we showed what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No new stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ

All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

They bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

It has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Feel free to drop us your score predictions in the comments – bragging rights on the line for the winner.

We’ll be bringing you team news, previews from the managers and more ahead of kick-off at 8pm!

#1085. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

DW has found that three-quarters of Russia's weightlifting team had no independent out-of-competition testing before this year's world championships, despite the country's doping history.

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."

WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

#1084. How to make AI data centres more sustainable

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

AI companies must engage with those who oppose the expansion of data centres.Credit: Michael M. Santiago/Getty

Around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency says.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

There are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

But none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that new energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

One solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

There is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

These are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

There are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

#1080. European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets

European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

#1078. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

#1076. What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship

As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark without Russia.

Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada said.
